## Objectives

- Grow a tree by hand: one split, one impurity calculation, one decision
- Understand why trees overfit on purpose, and how pruning fixes it
- Read a fitted tree the way a manager, or a clinician, can — because that is the point of them
- Set up Friday: why one tree is weak and a hundred are strong

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
The only model you can print on one page and hand to the people who must apply it
:::

| | One branch, read aloud | Who reads it, and argues |
|---|---|---|
| **Bank** | income < 30k and no prior account → *decline* | the credit committee, the regulator |
| **Hospital** | heart failure, two admissions this year, lives alone → *nurse call within 48 h of discharge* | the ward's doctors and nurses, the quality office |

: {tbl-colwidths="[16,52,32]"}

- Every branch is a **rule**. Every leaf is a **decision**. No coefficients, no link functions.
- Triage protocols and clinical pathways were trees long before machine learning. Now the data grow them, and a clinician can still disagree with a branch, and say which one

We are back to supervised learning. The $y$ is back. What changes is that the model is an **algorithm**, not an equation.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} Growing a tree {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## One question at a time

A tree splits the data with **yes/no questions on one variable**, recursively:

1. Look at all variables and all possible cut points
2. Choose the one split that makes the two resulting groups *purest*
3. Repeat inside each group
4. Stop when groups are small, or pure, or a depth limit is hit

The result partitions the predictor space into rectangles. Each rectangle gets one prediction: the majority class, or the mean of $y$.

::: {.callout-note}
"Purest" is where the whole method lives. For regression it is the residual sum of squares. For classification, two measures — next slide.
:::

## Measuring impurity

For a node with class proportions $p_1, \dots, p_K$:

- **Gini**: $\;G = \sum_k p_k (1 - p_k)$ — the probability two random draws disagree. Zero when pure.
- **Entropy**: $\;D = -\sum_k p_k \log p_k$ — zero when pure, maximal at even split.

A split is scored by the **weighted impurity of its two children**. The best split lowers it most. Both measures rank splits almost identically; `rpart` uses Gini by default.

## By hand: one split

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Ten customers, will they churn? Candidate: `tenure < 12 months`
:::

Parent node: 5 churn, 5 stay. $G = 2 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.50$

| | Churn | Stay | $G$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| tenure < 12 | 4 | 1 | $2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.32$ |
| tenure ≥ 12 | 1 | 4 | $0.32$ |

Weighted child impurity: $\tfrac{5}{10} \times 0.32 + \tfrac{5}{10} \times 0.32 = 0.32$.

**Gain: $0.50 - 0.32 = 0.18$.** Try `balance < 500` and get a gain of 0.02? Then tenure wins, the node splits on it, and the algorithm moves down to each child and starts again.

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} The first question of a screening tree

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · `MASS::Pima.tr`: 200 women, 68 diabetic, Gini 0.449
:::

| First split | Women, each side | Diabetic, each side | Gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| `glu < 123.5` (blood glucose) | 109 · 91 | 14% · 58% | 0.098 |
| `age < 28.5` | 104 · 96 | 15% · 54% | 0.075 |
| `npreg < 6.5` (pregnancies) | 159 · 41 | 26% · 66% | 0.052 |
| `bmi < 27.35` | 48 · 152 | 6% · 43% | 0.049 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,22,24,20]"}

1. Which split does `rpart` put at the root, and why?
2. The outreach van has a scale and a questionnaire but no lab: no `glu`. Which split starts its tree?
3. Is the van worth running? Tell the prevention manager in one sentence.

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Without a lab, start from age

- **Clinic**: `glu < 123.5`, the largest gain (0.098). Below it 14% are diabetic, above it 58%: the purest two groups any single question makes
- **Van**: `age < 28.5`, gain 0.075; `rpart` run without `glu` picks the same. 15% against 54%: almost the separation the blood test gives, so the van does not replace the clinic, it decides who goes there

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"Yes: without a blood test the van still splits the women into 15% and 54% diabetic, against 14% and 58% with one, so it screens on age and sends the women over 28 to the clinic for the glucose test."
:::

[Gain = 0.449 minus the Gini of the two sides, weighted. Without the lab the root loses 0.098 − 0.075 = 0.023 of its gain, about a quarter.]{.muted}

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Too far, and back {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## A fully grown tree is a lookup table

Left alone, the algorithm splits until every leaf is pure — with $n$ leaves for $n$ points if it has to.

- Training error: zero
- Test error: terrible. It has memorised the noise, one rectangle per accident
- This is **overfitting**, in its most visible form: you can *see* the absurd leaves

Trees are high-variance: change a few rows, get a different first split, get a different tree.

## Pruning: grow big, then cut back

Grow the full tree $T_0$. Then for a penalty $\alpha \ge 0$ find the subtree minimising

$$
\text{RSS}(T) \;+\; \alpha \,|T|
$$

where $|T|$ is the number of leaves. Larger $\alpha$: smaller tree. Choose $\alpha$ by **cross-validation** — the same logic as choosing $\lambda$ in LASSO, and for the same reason.

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
`rpart` does this for you, and prints the cross-validation table as `cptable`. Read it. Pick the `cp` at the minimum `xerror` — or the simplest tree within one standard error of it. The default tree it draws is *not* the pruned one.
:::

## In R

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4|6|8|10-11|13"}
library(tidyverse); library(rpart); library(rpart.plot); library(ISLR2)
d <- Default                                    # 10 000 credit-card customers; default yes/no

set.seed(1); tr <- sample(nrow(d), 7000)

fit <- rpart(default ~ balance + income + student, data = d[tr, ], method = "class")

printcp(fit)                                    # the cross-validation table

best <- fit$cptable[which.min(fit$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
pruned <- prune(fit, cp = best)

rpart.plot(pruned)                              # the one-page model
```

Then `predict(pruned, d[-tr, ], type = "class")` against `d$default[-tr]` — the confusion matrix — and you have a test error to report.

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} How much tree do the GPs get?

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · `printcp(fit)` for Drill 1's women, after `set.seed(16)`, turned on its side
:::

| `nsplit` | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CP` | 0.221 | 0.162 | 0.074 | 0.059 | 0.015 | 0.010 |
| `rel error` | 1.00 | 0.78 | 0.62 | 0.54 | 0.49 | 0.44 |
| `xerror` | 1.00 | 0.96 | 0.75 | 0.72 | 0.65 | 0.71 |
| `xstd` | 0.099 | 0.097 | 0.091 | 0.089 | 0.086 | 0.089 |

1. Which tree has the lowest `xerror`? How many leaves? (leaves = `nsplit` + 1)
2. The 1-SE rule: the smallest tree whose `xerror` is under the minimum plus its `xstd`. Which one?
3. The district's GPs will apply the tree on paper, at the desk. Which one do you print for them, and why?

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Four leaves, on paper

- **Minimum**: `xerror` 0.65 at 4 splits, **five leaves**. The default tree, 7 splits, fits these 200 women better (`rel error` 0.44) and new women worse (`xerror` 0.71)
- **1-SE**: 0.65 + 0.086 ≈ 0.74; the smallest tree under it has 3 splits, `xerror` 0.72: **four leaves**

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"The four-leaf tree: its cross-validated error is within one standard error of the best, so the data cannot tell the two apart, and a GP applies four leaves without a computer."
:::

[`xerror` is relative to the root's error, 68/200 = 0.34: 0.65 × 0.34 = 22% of women misclassified in cross-validation, 0.72 × 0.34 = 24.5%.]{.muted}

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Reading the tree {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Reading the tree you printed

- **Top node**: the single most useful question in the data. On `Default`, it is `balance < 1789`. One variable, and most of the signal.
- Each node shows the predicted class, the class probability, and the share of data reaching it
- A leaf with 2% of the data and a 51% probability is a leaf that should not exist — the pruning failed, or the `cp` was too small

::: {.callout-note}
Notice what is *not* in the tree: `student`. It was available, and no question about it ever beat one on `balance` or `income`. That is a finding, and it is free — about this tree, not yet about the world.
:::

## [Drill 3]{.drill-kicker} Read it to the clinic

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · Drill 2's four-leaf tree, as `print()` gives it · `ped` is a family-history score
:::

| Leaf | Path | Women | Diabetic | Predicts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | `glu < 123.5` | 109 | 15 · 14% | no |
| B | `glu ≥ 123.5` · `ped < 0.3095` | 35 | 12 · 34% | no |
| C | `glu ≥ 123.5` · `ped ≥ 0.3095` · `bmi < 28.65` | 11 | 3 · 27% | no |
| D | `glu ≥ 123.5` · `ped ≥ 0.3095` · `bmi ≥ 28.65` | 45 | 38 · 84% | yes |

: {tbl-colwidths="[8,52,12,16,12]"}

1. Read leaf D aloud: one sentence a GP understands, with its numbers
2. Leaf B predicts "no", yet 12 of its 35 women are diabetic. The district invites every "yes" to a confirmatory test. Do you invite B too?
3. Age was the runner-up root in Drill 1 and is not in this tree. What do you tell the clinic about age?

## [Drill 3 · answer]{.drill-kicker} The tree, the cut and the missing variable

- **D**: "Glucose 124 or more, a family-history score of 0.31 or more and a BMI of 28.65 or more: 38 of these 45 women were diabetic."
- **B**: invite them. The tree says "no" only because 34% is under 50%, and 0.5 is the software's default, not a clinical decision. On the 332 women of `MASS::Pima.te`, inviting B as well finds 67 diabetic women instead of 53: 28 more invitations, half of them to diabetic women
- **Age** matters: in the full tree it splits the low-glucose women into 5% and 31% diabetic. Pruning removed it because both sides predict "no" — it changed no prediction

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"Age is not needed by *this* tree, which is not the same as age not mattering: among women with glucose under 124, those over 28 are six times as often diabetic."
:::

## Trees: the honest scorecard

| | For | Against |
|---|---|---|
| Interpretability | unmatched — the model is the explanation | |
| Interactions | found automatically | |
| Scale, transformations | irrelevant — splits are ordinal | |
| Accuracy | | usually beaten by everything on Friday |
| Stability | | change the data a little, get a different tree |

The last two rows are one problem, and Friday's lecture is one answer: **many trees**.

## A tree is a model you can argue with, branch by branch. Keep that in mind on Friday, when you give it up.  {.statement}

## Before the lab

- Run today's block. Prune at the 1-SE `cp` instead of the minimum. How many leaves do you lose? Does test error move?
- Do you get Drill 2's table? `set.seed(16)`, then `rpart(type ~ ., data = MASS::Pima.tr, method = "class")` and `printcp()`
- Fit a tree on `customers.csv` with the k-means segment you built in the lab on Fri 13 Nov as the target. Which variable is at the top? Is that the variable *you* would have named the segments by?
- Bootstrap: `d[sample(nrow(d), replace = TRUE), ]` three times, three trees. Compare the top splits.
